title: Has this been happening more recently, or am I just noticing it more?...
transcript: It's pretty common for theatre people to make movies. There's a lot of crossover there. But there's a trend that I find particularly fascinating, which is when playwrights or theatre writers go into film directing. It's counterintuitive in the sense that the much more common or expected thing is for a theatre writer to go into screenwriting and a theatre director to go into film directing. And likewise, when a play or musical gets adapted to the screen, you would expect that the person directing it is either the person who directed it on stage or someone who is more from the film world. But in the last few years, we've had adaptations like is god is the father and the humans, which were directed by the playwright, even though the playwright didn't direct it when it was on stage. Then you have people like Celine Song or Annie Baker who are now writing and directing original films even though they don't really have any directing experience on stage. Martin Mcdonagh is another example of someone who's been doing that same split for a long time now. But the rest of these examples are all pretty recent. Recently we've also seen Lin-Manuel Miranda carving a very unusual path where he's about to direct his second stage to screen adaptation, both of which were musicals that he did not write. And on the flip side, I don't believe he's ever directed on stage. And what makes this trend even More fascinating is that all of the examples I just named have turned out to be very good at directing films. Dare I say they might even be better than a lot of the work we've seen from stage directors who have directed films, which happens relatively often with, I would say, mixed results. And even when they do produce good work on film, they're often not really leaving much of a stamp with their cinematic voice. I think Sam Mendes is maybe one of the most significant examples of a director who's been able to carve out a lot of a claim both on film and on stage. I know there are plenty of other examples, but I do think it's on the rare side. But anyway, I digress. I would be interested to hear theories as to why a lot of these playwrights who have never directed on stage are doing such good work directing on film. My best guess, as someone who is neither a writer or a director in either of these mediums, is that the old saying goes that film is a director's medium and theatre is a writer's medium. So maybe what we're seeing here is artists who are just very good at being the primary driving voice behind a project, whatever form that takes, in whatever medium they're working in.
